anchor: Second generation, bred for student logic. Structure from Code as Creative Medium (Levin and Brain, 2021): every chapter an assignment with a brief, precedents, a closed exercise and an open make at two depths. Macro frame from Form+Code (Reas, McWilliams, LUST, 2010): parts named by what code does to form, with Parameterize as a part of its own. Opening and structural queer argument from Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook (1925/1953) read 'in drag', as the 2023 application proposes; Albers's Interaction of Color (1963) as the method of every argument. Parents: c7_creative_medium (structure), c3_form_code, c4_klee_kandinsky.
title: Bodies in Seven Verbs: a sketchbook in drag, in code
thesis: You start where Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook starts: a point that goes for a walk. You write an instruction, give a body a time, decide with one 'if' whether it is solid, carry it, join two points with a line, keep your walk, and close it into a floor you stand on. By the end of the first week a machine has drafted one of your bodies, you have caught it, and you are standing among made and scanned bodies in the headset. From there the parts are named by what code does to a body, so you always know where you are. You REPEAT a body until many become one, colour it by a rule, let a seeded draw replace the rule, give it noise to stand on and run one function for every pixel. You PARAMETERIZE it: the families you have been making by hand become a type with exported fields, a sheet in the editor, a budget and a file. Then you TRANSFORM it (joints, scale, a weather), put it under FORCE (a gravity you write, a balance that fails, a ray that reaches, legs that drive from the foot, a swing you hear, a game), let rules GROW it, and finally LEAVE THE LAB, where the approximations fail in public before you make a body others may change. Each idea arrives when a body needs it: a line needs a function, a walk needs a list, a family needs a class, a fall needs a force. The order is related to Ada's spine but not forced by it: chance, noise and colour come earlier than the spine puts them because you need them in the first month and because regularity must exist for chance to be seen; Parameterize has no spine place at all; every departure is named where it happens, and the spine index below shows each one as a jump. In every chapter you build a body, vary one axis, write down before you render which two will look most alike, defend one sentence with the picture, say what the approximation owes or hides, and take the body where a person meets it. One thread is queer in the code itself: the scene tree's parent-commands-child is Klee's active-and-passive chain, and later you make the passive end drive. That kind of geometric and bodily critique has almost no precedent in critical code studies; this course is trying it.

parts.title: One body: the point goes for a walk (Klee I.1-4, Kandinsky)
parts.promise: You can write an instruction, build one body in code, give it a time, decide whether it is solid, carry it, relate it by a line, keep its walk, close the walk into a floor, check code a machine drafted for you, and stand among found and made bodies in the headset from a build you exported.

parts.title: Repeat: structure, colour, chance, noise, pixel (Klee I.5-8; Nake, Nees, Molnar)
parts.promise: You can make many bodies by a rule, colour them by a rule, let a seeded draw replace the rule, give them noise to stand on, and run one function for every pixel at once, and you can say what each repetition hides.

parts.title: Parameterize: the family as a type (an addition to the spine, declared)
parts.promise: You can write a body as a class whose exported fields make a family, sweep it into a comparison sheet in the editor, measure what each value costs, and save a body as a file someone else can build.

parts.title: Transform: joints, scale, weather (Klee I.9-12, II)
parts.promise: You can build a jointed body and name who commands whom, open the player body and read scale as a relation, and move many bodies by a field.

parts.title: Force and rhythm: to stand although it could fall (Klee II-IV)
parts.promise: Your bodies fall by gravity you wrote, balance and topple, reach by a ray, walk from the foot up, swing and sound, and play: a small complete game you export.

parts.title: Grow: rules that make bodies and worlds (NoC 7-9; WP2-3)
parts.promise: Bodies made by neighbour rules, recursion and grammars, bred by a fitness you write, a generated world searched as a graph, and a flock with no leader: procedures you can stop, save and argue with.

parts.title: Leave the lab: failure before futures (WP4; Queer 3D debt, then ontology)
parts.promise: Bodies that deform, fuse and learn, a model's limits made walkable, the course's own error measured, and a public body others may change.

tracks.title: Three weeks: a family in your own hall
tracks.length: 3 weeks in the Queer 3D format. Week 1 on the runnable kits: day 1 ch1+ch2, day 2 ch3+ch4, day 3 ch5+ch6, day 4 ch8, day 5 ch9 (scan brought from a day-1 afternoon scanning session; first export; headset). Week 2 one chapter a day: ch10, ch12, ch13, ch15, then day 10 with no new code: brief chosen, flowchart, peer review and a guest critique walk through the crisis halls. Week 3: making, one guest session, showing on the last day.
tracks.mini_project: A FAMILY IN DRAG. Choose one prompt: Virtual Creature, Parametric Object, Extrapolated Body, Personal Prosthetic, Generative Landscape, or The Body the Scanner Could Not See. Answer it with one class of your own with one @export axis of 3-5 values (ch15), optionally collaged with one scanned or Tilt Brush body (ch9), placed in your own hall where a visitor can stand on it, walk through it, carry it or become it, shown on desktop and once in the headset. Show your own sweep sheet with the prediction written and dated before rendering (which two members look most alike, and why), a one-sentence claim, and one debt comment in the code saying what the approximation owes. A prediction the render contradicts is worth the most. Supplied and named, because the short track skips their chapters or uses them before they are opened: the Day Zero base scene with the desktop walker and the XR rig (commons/scenes/vr_staging.tscn [V]); the point-zero, point-one, point-coordinates, point-lines and point-trace kits and the random-definition kit (doc/book/studies/ [V]); the segment helper (segment.gd, opened in ch7 of the long track); the collider and ball dropper (opened in ch7 and ch23); a column scene with its collider for the noise ground; one-line asides for what the short track skips: a colour from Color.from_hsv(i / float(n), 0.7, 0.9) (ch11), a floor from the walk (ch7), a shader (ch14). The sweep sheet is not supplied: students write it in ch15.

tracks.title: One year: from an instruction to a public body
tracks.length: about 42 weeks at one session a week: 38 chapters and 4 pause weeks with no new code idea (after Parts I, III, V and VI, as in Aesthetic Programming). Checkpoints close Parts I-III (ch9, ch14, ch18); the midterm game is ch27; the final is planned at ch36, two units before the end, and shown at ch38.
tracks.mini_project: Midterm: the One-Button Game (ch27) built from your own bodies, exported. Final: your hall in the class's collective museum (ch38): one family with its sweep sheet, the dated prediction, the claim, a debt comment in the code, a final.md drafted at ch36 (the argument, the prediction you got wrong, what your model cannot hold), your error column from ch37, an edit rule for visitors, and a headset build. Example axis, so the brief is not a placeholder: a soft pod family whose subdivisions (1, 2, 4, 8) decide where it can fold, predicted '4 and 8 look alike once settled', argued as 'deformation is paid for in polygons'.

chapters.title: Point Zero: a clock, and the engine calls you
chapters.body: A clock of primitives: a disc and one hand on a pivot. _ready places it once; _process turns the hand every frame from seconds accumulated with delta; one variable counts frames and another counts seconds, printed side by side.

argument.predict: After 60 s at a steady 60 fps all four agree. Run the same scene capped at 30 fps or at 90: delta seconds and the system clock stay together and look most alike, and the frame-count hand runs slow or fast.
argument.claim: A frame is not a unit of time; only a hand driven by delta or the clock keeps the same angle on every machine.

chapters.debt: Engine time is sampled: _process runs when the engine decides, and a headset changes what a frame is. Ada measured it: a swing damped per tick keeps 0.451 of its amplitude at 60 Hz and 0.294 at 90 Hz [V doc/book/iterations/claude-noc-vs-lineage-2026-09-29/README.md]. Whose time counts, the GPU's frames or the calendar's seconds?
chapters.place: Stand under a wall-sized clock in your room; set Engine.max_fps to 30 and then 90 and watch the frame-driven hand run away from the others.

argument.predict: With a ball dropped on each, equal and double look most alike at hall distance: a ball resting a few centimetres above a surface is hard to see. None (it falls through) and half (it sinks in) are obvious.
argument.claim: What you see and what holds you are two properties of one body; a body can look solid and be a ghost.

chapters.debt: The collider is a second, simpler body standing in for the first. Which bodies may be passed through is decided by one if, not by the mesh. Passing, looking like one thing and being another, is the first queer question a 3D engine asks, and it asks it with a boolean.

chapters.title: Point Trace: the walk that remains
chapters.body: A trace recorder: the carried point appends its position to an Array[Vector3] once it has moved further than a gate distance from the last kept point (list before append, condition before threshold); a for loop redraws the list as an ImmediateMesh line strip; at capacity the oldest point is dropped.

argument.predict: 0 and 2 cm look most alike (a smooth ribbon); 50 cm becomes a polyline with visible corners.
argument.claim: A trace is not the walk; it is the walk filtered by a rule, and the rule shows as corners.

chapters.debt: Continuity is faked from a list. The list forgets at capacity, a rule decides what counts as having moved, and standing still leaves no mark. Every recorded walk is a sampled walk, and sampling is a choice about which past counts.

argument.claim: A surface has a side: what you see of a plane is a promise its winding and normals make.

chapters.debt: Hidden-surface algorithms decide what exists for the eye (Gaboury): a one-sided plane is invisible from behind while its collider still stops you. The fan fails on a concave walk: the approximation owes the shape its dents. And opening the helper does not by itself tell you what it hid (Chun's 'sourcery' [mem; V-p LEARN.md]): the thin box passed as a line for two chapters.

chapters.title: Colour is a rule: Klee's central grey
chapters.body: A floor of pixel bodies you stand on: each tile a box with its own StandardMaterial3D whose albedo is computed from its index, between two complementary colours; a Dictionary keyed by Vector2i finds the tile under your feet and recolours it.

argument.axis: path between two complementary colours across nine tiles
argument.predict: RGB lerp and RGB stepped look most alike: the same straight path through the colour cube, one quantised, and both pass through Klee's central grey. The two HSV paths never go grey and differ only in which hues they cross.
argument.claim: The grey in the middle belongs to the RGB space, not to the colours: the same two ends give a grey or a rainbow.

chapters.debt: A colour on screen is a gamut, a tone map and a lamp, not a property of the body: the same albedo reads differently under Color_Flashlight. Albers's universal eye and Klee's colour spiritualism are claims to test. Film stock was calibrated to one skin tone (the Shirley card [mem]): the pixel has a politics.
chapters.place: Stand on it: the tile under your feet changes by the rule. Carry the flashlight and watch the surface change while the material does not.

chapters.title: Tile, rule, chance: Nake's Hommage a Paul Klee
chapters.body: A floor of tile bodies on the ch10 lattice, each one of two diagonal modules. First a rule decides, a boolean from the cell index ((i + j) % 2 == 0, a checker). Then chance decides: rng.randf() < p, the seed printed on a Label3D so the same seed returns the same maze. Long track: a Schotter wall follows, rotation and offset growing row by row.

argument.predict: 0.25 and 0.75 look most alike: mirror twins with the same amount of order in opposite directions. 0.5 is the most maze-like; 0 and 1 return to the rule's 'all the same'.
argument.claim: Chance has a dial: p sets how ordered the pattern is, and the seed only picks one member of that family.

chapters.debt: Pseudo-randomness: the numbers are a pattern that returns (Random_Definition). A seed makes chance repeatable, which is what lets you argue with it. Nake and Nees used random numbers in place of intuition: can a pseudo-random number stand in for a choice? In Schotter the rotation saturates at 45 degrees, because a square looks the same after a quarter turn: disorder is measured against the body's own symmetry.
chapters.place: Walk the maze at human scale: at p = 0.5 you can get lost; change the seed and it is another room with the same character.

chapters.title: Noise you can stand on
chapters.body: A landscape of column bodies: a column scene instanced on a grid, its height FastNoiseLite.get_noise_2d(x, z) times an amplitude; beside it the same grid with heights from randf(), so chance and noise stand side by side. The noise type can be simplex, Perlin, value or cellular (Voronoi). Supplied balls roll into the valleys.

argument.predict: 4 and 8 look most alike: each octave halves the amplitude, so after four the added detail is smaller than one column. 1 is the smooth blob landscape.
argument.claim: Noise is chance that remembers its neighbours; octaves add detail only down to the size of the bodies that show it.

chapters.debt: The blob aesthetic (Queer 3D intro [V QUEER3D.md]): Perlin and simplex noise made a whole era of 3D look alike. Noise is 'nature' chosen for being cheap and smooth; Palle's overflow comparison (Perlin 45, random 635, Voronoi 0, sine space 3284 [V QUEER3D.md]) shows how differently the families behave.

argument.claim: A parametric surface has a step count below which it is a different body and above which it is only cost: the check finds the first, the profiler the second.

argument.predict: 'At the end' and 'at one third' look most alike after 30 degrees; 'outside' makes the chain orbit instead of bend.
argument.claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like.

chapters.title: Flow field: a weather of bodies
chapters.body: A particle system of your own: positions in a PackedVector3Array advected every frame through a FastNoiseLite angle field (position += field(p) * delta, motion with no force yet), each particle reborn at the edge when its lifetime runs out, trails kept in a bounded buffer; then the same field driving a GPUParticles3D emitter, to compare.

argument.predict: 0.1 and 0.3 look most alike: above some frequency the trails turn into hair or fur, a texture rather than currents. 0.01 reads as one wind.
argument.claim: Below a frequency a flow field is a place you could be carried through; above it, it is a texture on the air.

chapters.debt: The field is noise again (the blob returns as wind), and particles exist only as long as a number you chose and the frame budget allow. Rate and accumulation (Change_Intro): a trail is an integral you draw. Moving position straight by a field skips mass entirely, which ch22 repairs.
chapters.place: Stand in the flow: particles stream around you. On the headset route the field carries the player slowly, with no rotation, and you learn why comfort is not polish.

chapters.title: A curve made of steps: your own gravity
chapters.body: A thrown body stepped by your own integrator in _physics_process: velocity += gravity * dt, position += velocity * dt (semi-implicit Euler), with an exported time step; the ch6 trace recorder draws the curve, and the engine's RigidBody3D is thrown beside it (supplied, opened in ch23).

argument.predict: 1/90 and 1/30 look most alike: both smooth arcs landing within a few centimetres of each other. 1/3 s shows corners in the trace and lands visibly off.
argument.claim: A simulated curve is a stack of straight steps; the size of the step decides where the body lands.

chapters.debt: Integration is an approximation that can gain or leak energy. The headset changes the step: XR Tools sets physics to the refresh rate, and Ada measured the same damped swing keeping 0.451 of its amplitude at 60 Hz against 0.294 at 90 Hz [V README]. One gravity for every body is a norm: Vectors_Act5 asks what a place with other laws would be.

chapters.title: Drawing Machine II: the harmonograph you can hear
chapters.body: A harmonograph: two damped pendulums written as sin and cos of time (phase, decay per second) drive a pen whose last N marks are kept in a bounded queue and drawn as one MultiMesh. Each pendulum is also a tone rendered into an AudioStreamWAV, so the figure's frequency ratio is heard as an interval; a world-space panel of sliders sets the ratio.

argument.axis: frequency ratio of the two pendulums
argument.predict: In the still at 60 s, 2:3 and 3:4 look most alike (both knotted, 3:4 denser); 1:1 is an ellipse; 1:1.01 slowly precesses into a rosette and, heard at 100 Hz, beats once a second.
argument.claim: Small whole-number ratios close their figure and sound consonant; a ratio one percent off never returns, and the drift is both the drawing and the beat.

chapters.debt: Damping written per frame breaks at 90 Hz: write decay per second. The sine is the 'pure' tone because Fourier made it the unit, and equal temperament makes every interval slightly out of tune, one musical culture's compromise. Audio runs on its own clock: a Timer on the frame clock drifts against the audio buffer. The queue forgets its oldest mark.
chapters.place: Walk around the drawing as it grows in the air; the tones come from the two bobs (AudioStreamPlayer3D), so the interval moves as you do.

chapters.title: One-Button Game: stand or sink (midterm)
chapters.body: A round made of your bodies: stones in a group 'stones' whose states IDLE, WARN, SINKING and GONE are switched by a seeded Timer; the opened walker or the XR body; one button (jump, or grab on the headset); a score and restart on the world-space panel; a sound per state; the best score saved to user://; exported.

argument.axis: warning time before a stone sinks
argument.predict: In a mid-round still, 1 s and 2 s look most alike: many stones wear warning rings and the player stands on a safe one. At 0 s no ring is ever visible.

chapters.title: Life: a rule for neighbours
chapters.body: A tower grown from a one-dimensional automaton: each generation a row of boxes computed from the row below by a rule number read as bits, with two buffers (current, next) swapped each step and one awaited step per generation; stacked upward, the history is a body you can climb. argument.predict: 30 and 110 look most alike from a distance (both irregular); 90 is a clean Sierpinski triangle and 184 a traffic of diagonals.
argument.claim: One byte of rule decides a whole body; neighbours make a form no single cell contains.

chapters.debt: The edge: the row wraps with (i + n) % n, a torus nobody sees. Without a second buffer cells read neighbours already updated, an order-of-evaluation bug that looks like a new rule. Rule 30 is chaos from order; Wolfram's classes are a taxonomy, not a law, and Life is not alive.

chapters.title: The tree and its grammar: a rule that must be stopped
chapters.body: A tree after Munari's rule: branch(pos, basis, length, depth) calls itself twice with a shorter, thinner child until depth reaches 0. Then the same tree written as a word: an axiom and a Dictionary of rules rewrite a String n times, read by a turtle whose [ and ] push and pop its state on an explicit stack. Recursion's hidden stack becomes one you can see.

argument.predict: 6 and 8 look most alike: each generation halves the branch, so depth 8's twigs are finer than the silhouette shows, at four times the nodes of depth 6.
argument.claim: An apparent infinity is a finite budget: past the depth the eye can resolve, recursion only spends.

chapters.debt: 'Recursion must always be controlled' (Queer 3D intro [V QUEER3D.md]): with no base case there is no tree, only a stack overflow. The string grows exponentially, so a symbol budget is a grammar's base case. Munari's 'mad branches' turn up in every family: the exception as the queer reading of the rule. Lindenmayer's plants are idealised: botany as a formal language.

argument.claim: Connectedness is not proportional to openness: near one probability a world snaps from islands to a continent.

chapters.debt: What counts as a connected, usable route? The navmesh is baked for one body radius: a wheelchair, a crawling body or a flying one gets another world. Which relation survives when the picture is rearranged (graph theory's question [V-p c7])?

learned_from: Code as Creative Medium (Levin and Brain) [V-p]: the chapter format: an open brief, precedent works that answered it before, a short closed exercise that trains one code idea, and an open make step at two depths (short and long track). Its body briefs (Parametric Object, Personal Prosthetic, Virtual Creature, Extrapolated Body, Virtual Public Sculpture, Data Self-Portrait, One-Button Game) name chapters here, and the interview theme 'When Things Go Wrong' names ch8.

Form+Code (Reas, McWilliams, LUST) [V-p]: parts named by what code does to form, so a student can always say where they are: Repeat, Parameterize, Transform, then force and growth. Parameterize is a part of its own (ch15-18) because 74% of Ada's scripts are @export families [V BRIEF.md] and every argument sweeps one.

Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook, read 'in drag' as the 2023 application proposes [V APPLICATION.md; Klee text V-p c4]: the opening walk (point, line, walk, plane) and the structural queer argument: the scene tree's parent-to-child command is Klee's active/passive (and male/female) chain (ch19), inverted by inverse kinematics so the passive end drives (ch25).
Albers, Interaction of Color [V-p]: every ARGUMENT is an Albers problem: one constrained material, one axis, a visible target, members compared side by side, a prediction written before the render.

Processing Handbook, 1st ed. [V-p]: two tables of contents (reading order and spine index, below), a Synthesis closing Parts I-III, and numbered returns (Drawing Machine II, Virtual Creature II; randomness returns as entropy).
10 PRINT [V-p]: regularity before randomness, so chance replaces a checker rule on a lattice the student built (ch12), and the maze becomes a place (ch12, ch31).

Aesthetic Programming (Soon and Cox) [V-p]: critique tied to the syntax that made the body, never a separate theory track; pause weeks; the final planned two units before the end; an open question kept beside every falsifiable number (ch37).

Critical code studies (Marino, CCSWG, Montfort) [V-p]: write first, read after; 'describe a body in a single class' (ch15); 'Critique My Starter Programs' turned on Godot's capsule (ch20); the marching-cubes table read as a code-critique station (ch34); a debt comment in the student's own code (ch38).

Chun's 'sourcery' [mem; placement V-p LEARN.md]: put in the debt step of the first chapter that opens a supplied helper (ch7, the segment 'line' that was a box) and again at the first machine draft (ch8).
Code Societies (SFPC, three weeks) [V-p]: the short track's third week with a guest session, and the crisis halls taught as a critique session beside code (ch36) rather than as more code.

The Nature of Code [V-p]: field before force (ch21 then ch22), the Mover and the integrator, oscillation, CA, fractals, evolution and agents as Parts V-VI; the Ecosystem Project as the model for the student's museum hall.

GDQuest and Godot's 'Your first 3D game' [V-p]: use before make, supplied parts declared and opened later (segment helper ch7, collider ch7, RigidBody ch23, walker ch20, FABRIK ch25); skin separate from controller so the desktop body can be swapped for the XR body.

Queer and feminist teaching (CCS 382, Queer Game Studies, Feminist Data Set, Blas) [V-p]: failure before futures (Part VII opens with deformation and the model's limits before the public body); consent and self-labelled data (ch35); the scanner's bias (ch9).

What the canon lacks [V-p LEARN.md]: no course found combines critique, writing code, 3D/VR bodies and art-school beginners. The canon's critique is social and linguistic; this course's geometric and bodily critique (polycount against deformation, the blob aesthetic, recursion that must be stopped, the one standpoint of an impossible body) has almost no precedent, and the thesis says so.

Queer 3D World 2024 (Palle's own course) [V QUEER3D.md]: the three layers (foundation, debt, ontology) in every chapter; its artistic lineage (Hoch, Bellmer, Bourgeois, Satterwhite, Perry, Kawaguchi, Kunz, Clark, Jansen, Reutersvard, blob architecture) replaces much of the canonical, mostly male precedent list the judges flagged in c7.
